Case Characteristics: 
1. Female patient, 19 years old.
2. The patient developed obvious obsessive-compulsive symptoms more than one year ago. After psychiatric diagnosis and pharmacological treatment, symptoms alleviated. Recently, she developed depression and lack of motivation in daily life, with impaired social functioning. Upon follow-up, diagnosed with simple type schizophrenia. Medication effect was suboptimal, leading to hospital admission from outpatient clinic.

History of Present Illness: 
More than one year ago, the patient experienced contamination fear, increased frequency of hand washing, and prolonged washing time. She exhibited compulsions and counter-compulsions, spoke softly, and spat. Symptoms lasted about one month before visiting a psychiatric clinic, where she was diagnosed with "obsessive-compulsive disorder" and treated with sertraline, escitalopram, clonazepam, and other medications. She adhered to treatment for about one year, with symptoms largely resolved, and discontinued medication on her own, with partial recovery of social function. Two months ago, she became apathetic, unwilling to wash, and dropped out of school to stay at home. Her mood was low, unable to feel happiness, with decreased interest. Seven days ago, she visited a hospital and was diagnosed with "simple type schizophrenia" and treated with amisulpride and sertraline, but the effect was poor. She was admitted from the outpatient clinic for further treatment.

Past Medical History: 
None reported.

Family History: 
None reported.

Physical Examination: 
Temperature 36.6℃, pulse 78 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, blood pressure 120/94 mmHg. Conscious and alert, breathing smooth, responses relevant, speech clear, cooperative during examination. No jaundice on skin or mucous membranes. No enlargement of superficial lymph nodes. Neck supple, no resistance, no jugular vein distention. Trachea midline. Chest normal shape, no widened intercostal spaces. Percussion of lungs resonant bilaterally. Breath sounds clear, no rales or wheezes heard. Cardiac borders normal on percussion. Heart rate 78 beats/min, regular rhythm, no murmurs. Abdomen flat, no tenderness or rebound tenderness. Liver and spleen not palpable. Negative hepatojugular reflux. No pitting edema in both lower limbs. Physiological reflexes present, pathological reflexes absent.

Mental Status Examination: 
  Appearance and Behavior: Conscious and alert, oriented correctly. Attention not concentrated. Answers relevant but voice low. Dress appropriate for occasion. Expression blank. Partial self-care in daily life. Limited interaction with surroundings, indifferent toward medical staff and family members.
  Mood Affect and Experience: Low mood, unable to feel happiness, decreased interest. Lack of insight.
  Cognition Thought and Perception: No auditory hallucinations, no other hallucinations, no delusions. Speech slow. Thought form disturbances: slowed thought and poverty of thought; no disorder of thought content. Normal common sense, intact judgment and comprehension. Impaired calculation ability. Normal recent and remote memory.

Ancillary Investigations: 
None reported.

Case Characteristics: 
1. Male patient, 14 years old.
2. The patient has exhibited reduced speech and movement, lack of communication with outsiders, reluctance to go out, and self-care ability for over 1 year. Two months ago, he developed fear of strangers, stayed at home all day, refused to go outside, showed no negative behaviors, and could communicate with family members. Recently, family members reported that the patient talks to himself, points at the air while cursing, and claims to hear voices insulting him, said to be classmates and neighbors, but no one is visible. Ten days ago, he experienced headache, rhinorrhea, and elevated body temperature; symptoms alleviated after treatment at a local hospital. At school, he still does not interact with others and sits alone on the rooftop. Currently, his contact with the outside world is poor, he does not respond when asked, and he presented to our outpatient department today.

History of Present Illness: 
The patient began to show reduced speech and movement, lack of communication with outsiders, and reluctance to go out but maintained self-care over 1 year ago. Two months prior, he developed fear of strangers, stayed home all day, refused outdoor activities, exhibited no obvious negative behaviors, and could communicate with family. Family members reported that he claimed to hear voices insulting him, identified as classmates and neighbors, but no one is seen; he frequently talks to himself and points at the air while cursing. Ten days ago, he developed headache, rhinorrhea, and fever around 38°C; symptoms improved after treatment at a local hospital without detailed examination, and medication details are unclear. At school, he still avoids contact with others and sits alone on the rooftop. Currently, the patient has poor interaction with the outside world, does not respond to questions, and presented to our outpatient department today.

Past Medical History: 
Denies history of seizures, nausea, vomiting, or hemiplegia. Denies history of diabetes. Denies epilepsy history. Denies history of surgeries or blood transfusions.

Family History: 
Denies family history of psychiatric disorders within three generations. Denies significant hereditary diseases.

Physical Examination: 
Temperature 36.5°C, pulse 82 beats/min, respiration 20 breaths/min, blood pressure 111/73 mmHg. Patient is conscious. Breathing is stable. No jaundice on skin or mucous membranes. Several lymph nodes palpable in the neck and groin. Neck supple without resistance. No jugular venous distention. Trachea midline. Chest normal without widened intercostal spaces. Percussion of lungs reveals clear resonance bilaterally. Breath sounds clear without rales or wheezing. Cardiac percussion borders normal. Heart rate 82 beats/min, regular rhythm, no murmurs. Abdomen flat without tenderness or rebound pain. Liver and spleen not palpable below ribs. Negative hepatojugular reflux. No pitting edema in both lower limbs.

Mental Status Examination: 
  Appearance and Behavior: Conscious, appropriately dressed, partially self-care capable, no interaction with surroundings, uncooperative during mental examination.
  Mood Affect and Experience: Inner experience inaccessible, poor engagement.
  Cognition Thought and Perception: According to family reports, the patient exhibits possible auditory hallucinations (hearing voices insulting him, identified as classmates and neighbors but unseen), frequently talks to himself, and points at the air while cursing.

Ancillary Investigations: 
Brain CT on 2012-09-05 at our hospital showed no significant abnormalities. Chest X-ray indicated no obvious abnormalities in heart and lungs, with slight adhesion on the left diaphragm surface.

Case Characteristics: 
1. Female patient, 28 years old.
2. Five years ago, the patient suddenly developed acute symptoms including palpitations and whole-body tremors, which were relieved after medication; symptoms recurred intermittently and could be alleviated by self-medication.
3. Three years ago, the patient began experiencing low mood and decreased energy and sought medical consultation.

History of Present Illness: 
Five years ago, the patient suddenly experienced palpitations, whole-body tremors, and a feeling of impending death. A Holter monitor performed at an external hospital showed no significant abnormalities. Symptoms were relieved after oral administration of Alprazolam. Since then, these symptoms have frequently recurred and could be relieved by self-administered Alprazolam. Three years ago, the patient began to frequently feel depressed and subjectively lacked energy, prompting her to seek treatment at our hospital.

Past Medical History: 
The patient’s general health condition has been average. She has a history of hyperthyroidism.

Family History: 
None reported.

Physical Examination: 
Temperature 36.6℃, pulse 75 beats/min, respiration 20 breaths/min, blood pressure 115/75 mmHg. The patient was conscious and alert, breathing steady, responses appropriate and coherent, speech clear, cooperative during examination. No jaundice of skin or mucous membranes. No enlargement of superficial lymph nodes. Neck supple without resistance, no jugular venous distension. Trachea midline. Thorax normal without widened intercostal spaces. Percussion of both lungs revealed clear resonance; breath sounds clear without rales or wheezing. Cardiac borders not enlarged on percussion; heart rate 75 beats/min, regular rhythm, no murmurs. Abdomen flat, no tenderness or rebound tenderness; liver and spleen not palpable. Negative hepatojugular reflux sign. No pitting edema in both lower limbs. Physiological reflexes present; pathological reflexes not elicited.

Mental Status Examination: 
  Appearance and Behavior: Clear consciousness, good spirit, cooperative and relevant responses during questioning.
  Mood Affect and Experience: Anxious and suspicious mood, subjective report of poor energy and high stress, willpower intact, denies suicidal ideation.
  Cognition Thought and Perception: Denies hallucinations, delusions, or other psychotic symptoms. Attention is somewhat impaired. Insight intact. General knowledge, judgment, comprehension, and calculation abilities are normal.

Ancillary Investigations: 
None reported.

Case Characteristics: 
1. Female patient, 26 years old.
2. Chief complaints: Sudden onset of dizziness 5 years ago, causing anxiety, gradually followed by depressive mood and inability to feel happiness, with severe cases showing reduced interest and activity. Accompanied by poor sleep quality. Frequent unexplained episodes of fear and despair, hopelessness about the future, excessive worry and distress about her illness and physical health. Previously diagnosed with "depression" at a large hospital and treated with venlafaxine, with symptom relief; medication was discontinued after more than one year of treatment. Over one year ago, she developed neck pain and was diagnosed with "bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy" at this hospital, with no improvement after medication. Later diagnosed with "left submandibular lymphadenitis" at another hospital, with no improvement after anti-infective treatment. The patient began to feel anxious and fearful, worried about her health, gradually developing low mood, inability to feel happiness, irritability, loss of emotional control, and difficulty concentrating. Admitted to hospital outpatient clinic with diagnosis of "depression." No episodes of elevated mood, excitement, or talkativeness during the course of illness.

History of Present Illness: 
Five years ago, the patient experienced sudden dizziness which caused anxiety, gradually developing depressive mood and inability to feel happiness, with severe cases showing reduced interest and activity. Accompanied by poor sleep quality. She often experienced unexplained fear and despair, hopelessness about the future, and excessive worry and distress about her illness and physical health. She was diagnosed with "depression" at a large hospital and treated with venlafaxine (specific maximum dose unknown), resulting in some symptom relief. She adhered to medication for more than one year and discontinued treatment as per medical advice after complete symptom remission. More than one year ago, she developed neck pain and was diagnosed with "bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy" at this hospital; medication was given (details unknown) with no improvement. Later, diagnosed with "left submandibular lymphadenitis" at another hospital; anti-infective treatment was ineffective. The patient began to feel anxious and fearful, worried about her health, gradually developing low mood, inability to feel happiness, irritability, loss of emotional control, and difficulty concentrating. She was admitted to hospital outpatient clinic with a diagnosis of "depression." No symptoms of elevated mood, excitement, or excessive talking were observed during the illness.

Past Medical History: 
The patient’s general health condition is average. She experienced mild concussion after a fall in 2000 and was diagnosed with "myocarditis" two years ago.

Family History: 
None reported.

Physical Examination: 
Temperature 36.8℃, pulse 92 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, blood pressure 104/70 mmHg. Conscious and alert, breathing smooth, responses appropriate and coherent, clear speech, cooperative during examination. No jaundice on skin or mucous membranes. Bilateral cervical and submandibular superficial lymphadenopathy present. Neck soft without resistance, no jugular vein distension, trachea midline, normal thorax, no widened intercostal spaces. Percussion of both lungs reveals clear resonance, breath sounds clear without rales or wheezing. Cardiac borders not enlarged on percussion, heart rate 92 beats per minute, regular rhythm, no murmurs. Abdomen flat without tenderness or rebound tenderness, liver and spleen not palpable. Negative hepatojugular reflux sign. No pitting edema in both lower extremities. Physiological reflexes present, pathological reflexes absent.

Mental Status Examination: 
  Appearance and Behavior: Conscious and alert, oriented, attention not focused, responses appropriate, appearance consistent with age. Appropriate clothing, sad facial expression, independent in daily living. Social functioning partially impaired.
  Mood Affect and Experience: Mood: anxious, depressed; decreased interest; irritability; easy fatigability; no auditory hallucinations; no other hallucinations; no delusions.
  Cognition Thought and Perception: Normal common sense, judgment and comprehension intact, normal calculation ability. Insight preserved.

Ancillary Investigations: 
In October 2012, a parotid and cervical lymph node ultrasound at a large hospital showed abnormal hypoechoic areas lateral to the bilateral submandibular glands below the parotid glands. In November 2012, cervical ultrasound at another hospital revealed a hypoechoic nodule in the left parotid gland and slight enlargement of bilateral submandibular, cervical, and submental lymph nodes. In March 2013, cervical ultrasound re-examination at a third hospital showed enlargement of the left submandibular gland and hypoechoic nodular shadows beside the large blood vessels of the left neck. In April 2013, physical examination at a fourth hospital indicated bilateral mammary gland hyperplasia, sinus arrhythmia, increased lung markings in both lungs, cystic space-occupying lesion of the left kidney, and urine occult blood 3+. On August 21, 2013, this hospital performed blood routine, thyroid function tests, brain CT, and EEG, all showing no significant abnormalities.

Case Characteristics: 
1. Male patient, 29 years old.
2. More than 2 years before admission, presented with palpitations, chest tightness, dizziness, dyspnea, and sweating; experienced mood depression, decreased interest, and cognitive decline; had a suicide attempt by jumping from a height; repeatedly visited multiple hospitals. Symptoms recurred after effective medication treatment. Admitted to our department from outpatient clinic with diagnosis of "Mood Disorder, Depressive Episode, Panic Attack."

History of Present Illness: 
More than 2 years before admission, the patient developed palpitations, chest tightness, dizziness, dyspnea, and sweating shortly after receiving clarithromycin for a cold, symptoms relieved in minutes but recurred repeatedly. Loud speaking and coughing by others easily triggered episodes. Gradually developed depressed mood, inability to feel happiness, decreased interest, subjective memory decline, and slowed response; previously no difficulty solving math problems but now some problems require much longer time. Severe anxiety led to suicide attempt by jumping from height. Multiple visits to various hospital departments with multiple examinations showing no abnormalities. Two years ago, an endocrinologist prescribed "Duloxetine 2 tablets once daily," which significantly relieved symptoms. Dosage was tapered monthly by half a tablet; symptoms relapsed after discontinuation but improved after resuming duloxetine. Symptoms recurred repeatedly, with intermittent medication. For further treatment, patient visited our outpatient clinic today and was admitted with diagnosis of "Mood Disorder, Depressive Episode, Panic Attack." Since onset, appetite is normal, consciousness clear, mental status fair, sleep fair, normal bowel and urinary function, and no significant weight change.

Past Medical History: 
Patient generally in average health. Hyperlipidemia detected, managed with dietary control. Underwent midline abdominal hernia surgery 13 years ago in a hospital, and fibroma excision on the forehead in the same year. Denies history of epilepsy, major somatic diseases, blood transfusions, or infectious diseases.

Family History: 
Denies family history of psychiatric disorders.

Physical Examination: 
T 36.6℃, P 80 beats/min, R 20 breaths/min, BP 110/76 mmHg. Conscious, breathing smooth, coherent responses, clear speech, cooperative during examination. No jaundice on skin or mucosa. No superficial lymphadenopathy. Neck supple without resistance, no jugular venous distention. Trachea midline, normal thorax without widened intercostal spaces. Percussion of lungs resonance clear; breath sounds clear without rales or wheezing. Cardiac percussion shows no enlargement; heart rate 80 beats/min, regular rhythm, no murmurs. Abdomen flat, about 6 cm surgical scar above umbilicus, no tenderness or rebound tenderness, liver and spleen not palpable. Negative hepatojugular reflux sign. No pitting edema in lower limbs. Physiological reflexes present; pathological reflexes absent.

Mental Status Examination: 
  Appearance and Behavior: Consciousness clear, orientation intact, attention focused, answers relevant, age-appropriate appearance. Appropriate clothing, sad facial expression, self-care intact. Social functioning severely impaired.
  Mood Affect and Experience: Mood: anxious, depressed, affect blunted; no auditory hallucinations or delusions.
  Cognition Thought and Perception: Partial insight. Normal common sense, impaired judgment and comprehension, normal calculation ability.

Ancillary Investigations: 
On 2011-10-21, SCL-90 showed highest scores in depression, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive, somatization, and sensitivity. Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale total score was 20, indicating definite anxiety. Hamilton Depression Rating Scale total score was 21, indicating moderate depression.

Case Characteristics: 
1. Male patient, 17 years old.
2. Over one year ago, the patient developed depressed mood. Eight months ago, he experienced unnecessary worries without obvious cause, accompanied by slowed thinking, lack of motivation, lethargy, and even inability to care for himself. Five months ago, he developed cleanliness obsession, repeatedly looking at his hands and washing them according to specific procedures; in severe cases, he washed his hands over 20 times, lasting more than 20 minutes each time. He felt these actions were unnecessary but felt compelled to perform them, causing significant distress. The patient's family brought him to a hospital where he was diagnosed with "Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder" and treated with sertraline 50mg once daily and olanzapine 5mg at bedtime, with fluctuating condition.

History of Present Illness: 
The patient developed depressed mood over one year ago. Eight months ago, without obvious cause, he began to experience unnecessary worries, accompanied by slowed thinking, lack of motivation, lethargy, and eventual inability to care for himself. Five months ago, he developed an obsession with cleanliness, repeatedly inspecting his hands and washing them according to specified steps; in severe episodes, he washed over 20 times per session, lasting more than 20 minutes. He recognized these behaviors as unnecessary but felt compelled to perform them, causing significant distress. His family brought him to a hospital where he was diagnosed with "Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder" and treated with sertraline 50mg once daily and olanzapine 5mg at night, with condition fluctuating.

Past Medical History: 
The patient's family denies history of seizures, nausea, vomiting, or hemiplegia. The patient denies history of hypertension. Denies history of diabetes mellitus.

Family History: 
None reported.

Physical Examination: 
Temperature 37 ℃, pulse 80 beats/min, respiration 20 breaths/min, blood pressure 201/80 mmHg. Conscious and alert, breathing smooth, responses appropriate, speech clear, cooperative during examination. No jaundice on skin or mucous membranes. No enlargement of superficial lymph nodes. Neck supple without resistance, no jugular venous distention. Trachea midline. Chest normal without widened intercostal spaces. Percussion of lungs reveals clear resonance; breath sounds clear without rales or wheezes. Cardiac percussion shows no enlargement of cardiac border; heart rate 80 beats/min, regular rhythm, no murmurs. Abdomen flat, no tenderness or rebound tenderness, liver and spleen not palpable. Negative hepatojugular reflux sign. No pitting edema in lower extremities.

Mental Status Examination: 
  Appearance and Behavior: Conscious and alert, orientation intact, attention focused, answers relevant, voice low. Clothing appropriate for season, expression blank, partially self-caring, passive in interactions with surroundings, indifferent toward medical staff and family.
  Mood Affect and Experience: Depressed mood, anxious, slowed thinking, slow speech.
  Cognition Thought and Perception: Lack of insight, no auditory hallucinations, no other hallucinations, no delusions. Formal thought disorder: poverty of thought, incoherent thinking; content of thought intact. Normal common sense, judgment, comprehension, calculation, recent and remote memory.

Ancillary Investigations: 
None reported.

Case Characteristics: 
1. Male patient, 10 years and 8 months old.
2. According to family, six months prior to admission, the patient developed paroxysmal crying episodes after being reprimanded and hit on the head by a teacher. He heard voices (classmates) calling him, mocking him for being hit by the teacher, and saying the teacher did not like him. These symptoms mainly occurred during headaches. The patient was irritable, kicked people or objects nearby, had poor sleep at night with difficulty falling asleep, frequent dreams, and easy awakening. He was treated at a local hospital and diagnosed with "stress disorder," receiving symptomatic supportive treatment with valproate magnesium 125 mg twice daily and risperidone 0.5 mg at night, which improved symptoms but auditory hallucinations persisted intermittently. One week before admission, the patient’s condition worsened, refusing to eat, claiming the food was poisoned though he did not know by whom. He denied being monitored or followed. He reported that seeing white walls triggered many thoughts, then he would see dinosaurs on the walls and believed this was supposed to happen. Sleep worsened, with sleep onset delayed to 2-3 a.m., appetite decreased, and weight loss occurred.
Five months prior to admission, abnormal findings were noted on urinalysis at a local hospital; after medication, partial improvement was seen upon re-examination.

History of Present Illness: 
Six months before admission, after being reprimanded and struck on the head by a teacher, the patient exhibited paroxysmal crying, auditory hallucinations of classmates calling him and mocking the teacher’s punishment, and the perception that the teacher disliked him. These symptoms mainly appeared during headaches. He became irritable and kicked nearby people or objects. Nighttime sleep was poor with difficulty falling asleep, frequent dreams, and easy awakening. At a local hospital, he was diagnosed with "stress disorder" and treated with valproate magnesium 125 mg twice daily and risperidone 0.5 mg nightly, which improved symptoms but intermittent auditory hallucinations remained. One week before admission, the condition deteriorated; he refused food, stating it was poisoned without knowing by whom. He denied surveillance or tracking. He reported that seeing snow-white walls triggered many thoughts, followed by visual hallucinations of dinosaurs on the walls, which he believed should appear. Sleep worsened, with sleep onset delayed to 2-3 a.m., decreased appetite, and weight loss. Five months before admission, urinalysis at a local hospital showed RBC 171/μL; urinary tract ultrasound was unremarkable. He was treated with Hematuria Capsules 1.4 g three times daily and Bailing Capsules 2 capsules three times daily, with follow-up urinalysis showing RBC 38/μL.

Past Medical History: 
None reported.

Family History: 
None reported.

Physical Examination: 
Temperature 36.5℃, pulse 85 beats/min, respiration 20 breaths/min, blood pressure 105/58 mmHg. Patient was conscious and clear-headed, breathing steady, responses appropriate and clear speech, cooperative during examination. Skin and mucous membranes showed no jaundice. No superficial lymphadenopathy. Neck supple without resistance, no jugular vein distension. Trachea midline. Chest normal without intercostal space widening. Percussion of lungs revealed clear resonance, breath sounds clear without rales or wheezing. Cardiac percussion showed no enlargement; heart rate 85 beats/min, regular rhythm, no murmurs. Abdomen flat, no tenderness or rebound tenderness, liver and spleen not palpable. Negative hepatojugular reflux sign. No pitting edema in both lower limbs. Physiological reflexes present, pathological reflexes absent.

Mental Status Examination: 
  Appearance and Behavior: Conscious and oriented. Attention was poor. Responses relevant but voice was low. Clothing appropriate for season, natural facial expression. Partial self-care in daily life. Passive interaction with surroundings, indifferent to medical staff and family members.
  Mood Affect and Experience: Lacked insight. Experienced auditory hallucinations (hearing people calling him, saying the teacher disliked him, and that he was naughty); visual hallucinations present; no delusions.
  Cognition Thought and Perception: Speech slow. No formal thought disorder. Thought content disordered with presence of referential and persecutory delusions. General knowledge normal. Judgment and comprehension intact. Calculation normal. Immediate and remote memory normal.

Ancillary Investigations: 
September 2, 2013, urinalysis at a certain hospital showed red blood cells 325/μL, white blood cells 69/μL. Acid-fast bacilli and PCR tests of urine were negative. Bilateral renal ultrasound did not support nephrolithiasis. Bladder ultrasound showed no significant abnormalities.

Case Characteristics: 
1. Male patient, 25 years old.
2. Three days ago, after his girlfriend left, he began drinking alcohol, followed by abnormal mental and behavioral symptoms (such as irrelevant talking, calling his girlfriend's name intermittently, wanting to play cards, refusal to eat, wandering around, unprovoked cursing, forcefully pulling his own nose and mouth with his hands, and talking to himself). He was admitted to our open ward from the emergency department with a diagnosis of "abnormal mental behavior."

History of Present Illness: 
Three days ago, after the patient’s girlfriend left, he started drinking alcohol in an unknown amount and developed abnormal mental and behavioral symptoms, including irrelevant talking, calling his girlfriend's name intermittently, wanting to play cards, refusing to eat, wandering aimlessly, unprovoked cursing, forcefully pulling his own nose and mouth with his hands, and talking to himself. He was brought to our hospital’s emergency department. Blood routine and electrolytes showed no significant abnormalities. Liver function tests revealed total bilirubin 47.0 µmol/L, indirect bilirubin 44.3 µmol/L, lactate dehydrogenase 642 U/L. Renal function showed uric acid 612 µmol/L. Cranial CT showed no obvious abnormalities. He was admitted to our open ward from the emergency department with a diagnosis of "abnormal mental behavior."

Past Medical History: 
None reported.

Family History: 
None reported.

Physical Examination: 
Temperature 36.8℃, pulse 92 beats/min, respiration 20 breaths/min, blood pressure not recorded. Neurological examination: patient was basically conscious and cooperative during physical examination. Pupils approximately 3 mm bilaterally, neck supple, no facial paralysis, normal muscle strength and muscle tone in all four limbs, no pathological reflexes elicited. Deep tendon reflexes ++ + in both upper limbs and ++ + in both lower limbs. No obvious abnormalities detected in heart, lungs, or abdomen.

Mental Status Examination: 
  Appearance and Behavior: The patient was clear-minded but had poor contact, reluctant to reveal inner thoughts, answered few questions, often curled up alone on the floor or bed, and emitted a voice resembling that of a woman.
  Mood Affect and Experience: Poor sleep, adequate food intake.
  Cognition Thought and Perception: Loss of insight and social functioning.

Ancillary Investigations: 
Blood routine and electrolytes showed no significant abnormalities. Liver function tests: total bilirubin 47.0 µmol/L, indirect bilirubin 44.3 µmol/L, lactate dehydrogenase 642 U/L. Renal function showed uric acid 612 µmol/L. Cranial CT showed no obvious abnormalities.

Case Characteristics: 
1. Female patient, 27 years old.
2. Main manifestations: Over one month ago, she developed chest tightness, shortness of breath, suffocation sensation, hypoxia, palpitations, and a feeling of impending death without obvious triggers. She felt dizzy while walking but remained conscious. Each episode lasted 2-3 hours. During attacks, mood was poor, unable to feel happiness, irritable, disinterested in playing mahjong, and felt so uncomfortable as if life was unbearable. Between attacks, she was completely normal. She was hospitalized multiple times at local and another hospital with recurrent episodes occurring 3-4 times daily, each lasting 1-2 hours and resolving spontaneously. Treatment with Deanxit and Olanzapine led to slight improvement. Recently, symptoms recurred after a quarrel with family, with reduced frequency and severity of attacks, decreased interest in activities, memory decline, and poor sleep. Admitted to our department for further treatment under the diagnosis of "anxiety and depressive state."

History of Present Illness: 
More than one month ago, the patient developed chest tightness, shortness of breath, suffocation sensation, hypoxia, palpitations, and a feeling of impending death without obvious triggers. She felt dizzy while walking but was conscious. Each episode lasted about 2-3 hours. During attacks, her mood was poor, unable to feel happiness, irritable, disinterested in mahjong, and felt so uncomfortable as if life was unbearable. Interictal periods were completely normal. She was hospitalized for one week at a local hospital. Tests including cardiac ultrasound, cranial CT, Holter monitoring, and cervical spine X-ray showed no significant abnormalities. Chest X-ray showed increased pulmonary markings. Symptomatic treatment (details unknown) was ineffective, and episodes recurred frequently, about 3-4 times per day, each lasting 1-2 hours and resolving spontaneously. She was hospitalized for one week at another hospital. Abdominal ultrasound, blood routine, liver and kidney function, blood glucose, electrolytes, routine urine and stool tests, and OGTT were all normal. Symptomatic treatment with Deanxit and Olanzapine led to slight improvement. Eleven days ago, after a quarrel with family, symptoms including fatigue, chest tightness, impending death sensation, dry mouth, and throat discomfort reappeared but with reduced frequency and severity. She experienced decreased interest in activities, memory decline, and poor sleep. She was hospitalized for 5 days at another hospital with no significant improvement. For further treatment, she was admitted to our department with a diagnosis of "anxiety and depressive state."

Past Medical History: 
The patient’s general health condition has been average. In 2000, she underwent surgery for ectopic pregnancy and received blood transfusion; details are unclear. She denies history of epilepsy, major somatic diseases, or infectious diseases.

Family History: 
Denies family history of psychiatric disorders.

Physical Examination: 
Temperature 36.5℃, pulse 75 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg. Conscious and alert, breathing smooth, responses appropriate and clear speech, cooperative during examination. No jaundice of skin or mucosa, no enlargement of superficial lymph nodes. Neck supple without resistance or jugular venous distension. Trachea midline. Chest shape normal without widened intercostal spaces. Percussion of lungs showed clear resonance; breath sounds clear without rales or wheezes. Cardiac percussion showed no enlargement. Heart rate 75 beats/min, regular rhythm, no murmurs. Abdomen flat, no tenderness or rebound pain. Liver and spleen not palpable. Negative hepatojugular reflux sign. No pitting edema in lower limbs. Physiological reflexes present; pathological reflexes absent.

Mental Status Examination: 
  Appearance and Behavior: Conscious, oriented, attentive, responses relevant, appearance consistent with age. Clothing appropriate, anxious facial expression, independent in self-care. Social functioning partially impaired.
  Mood Affect and Experience: Mood: anxious, depressed, low affect, irritable; no auditory hallucinations or other hallucinations.
  Cognition Thought and Perception: Insight intact, normal common sense, judgment and comprehension normal, calculation ability normal.

Ancillary Investigations: 
At a hospital in January 2012: abdominal ultrasound, blood routine, liver and kidney function tests, blood glucose, electrolytes, routine urine and stool tests, and oral glucose tolerance test showed no significant abnormalities. Our hospital’s data not yet available.

Case Characteristics: 
1. Female patient, 23 years old.
2. The patient developed psychiatric symptoms 8 years before admission after a failed confession of love; symptoms worsened over 2 years ago (after university graduation); 9 months ago symptoms improved after hospitalization at another hospital; symptoms worsened again 3 months ago.

History of Present Illness: 
Eight years prior to admission, the patient began to feel that others disliked her after a failed confession of love. She felt extremely inferior, was very nervous during social interactions, unable to relax, and worried that others would dislike her, gradually leading to avoidance of contact with others. More than 2 years ago (after university graduation), she was unwilling to work, barely communicated with others, and spent most of her time sleeping at home or surfing the internet. She became easily irritable, had unprovoked outbursts of anger, showed clear hostility towards her parents, frequently quarreled with them, and became irritable and threw objects at home if her parents did not comply with her demands. She was impervious to any persuasion and occasionally talked to herself. Nine months ago, she was hospitalized for 40 days in another hospital, where, after a multidisciplinary case discussion, she was diagnosed with “anxiety disorder, personality defects, and social dysfunction,” and treated with medications including Sertraline and Aripiprazole, leading to symptom improvement and discharge. She adhered to medication for one month after discharge, then discontinued; symptoms remained stable for 3 months after stopping. Three months ago, her relationship with her parents deteriorated again, with repeated disputes over many verbal matters with her mother, became overly sensitive to others’ questions related to her, showed occasional impulsive and irritable behaviors, and was hostile towards her parents in the past 7 days.

Past Medical History: 
The patient’s general health status is average. She denies epilepsy, other major somatic diseases, history of blood transfusion, and infectious diseases.

Family History: 
Denies family history of psychiatric disorders.

Physical Examination: 
Temperature 36.4℃, pulse 75 beats/min, respiration 20 breaths/min, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg. Conscious and alert, breathing steady, responses appropriate and relevant, speech clear, cooperative during examination. No jaundice of skin or mucosa. No enlargement of superficial lymph nodes. Neck supple without resistance, no jugular venous distension. Trachea midline. Chest normal shape without widened intercostal spaces. Percussion of both lungs resonant; breath sounds clear; no rales or wheezes heard. Cardiac border not enlarged on percussion; heart rate 75 beats/min, regular rhythm, no murmurs. Abdomen flat, no tenderness or rebound tenderness. Liver and spleen not palpable. Negative hepatojugular reflux. No pitting edema in both lower limbs. Physiological reflexes present; pathological reflexes absent.
